entities.summary: Jehovah's Witnesses was founded in 1881 by Charles Taze Russell, a Pittsburgh-based minister who sought to create a Christian movement based on the Bible's literal interpretation. The organization's early years were marked by Russell's efforts to establish a global presence, culminating in the organization's first convention in 1886. The group's name was officially adopted in 1895, following a 1914 event known as the 'Time of the End,' which predicted the imminent return of Christ and the eventual destruction of the world. Jehovah's Witnesses has since become a major player in global Christianity, with a presence in over 240 countries and territories. The group's distinctive practices, including door-to-door evangelism and the use of blood transfusions, have been the subject of controversy and debate. Despite this, Jehovah's Witnesses remains a significant force in modern Christianity, with an estimated 8.5 million adherents worldwide. The organization's headquarters, located in Warwick, New York, serves as a hub for its global operations, while its publication, The Watchtower, provides a daily devotional and news service to its members.
